lessons.title: REITs and InvITs: Alternative Assets With Listed Market Behaviour

children.text: There are two ways to own a piece of a Bengaluru tech park leased to global companies. You can buy a fractional share of one building through a platform, with an occasional valuation and no easy exit. Or you can buy units of a listed REIT on NSE, which owns many such buildings, pays you every quarter, and can be sold the next trading day. The buildings are equally real either way. What changes is the behaviour: the REIT hands you daily liquidity and a visible price, and in return, that price swings with the stock market and with interest rates. This lesson profiles that hybrid, and its cousin the InvIT, where a high yield can hide a very different kind of return.

body.text: REITs and InvITs are three assets in one wrapper: property or infrastructure cash flows underneath, bond-like distributions on top, and a stock-like price in between. You give up the comfort of smooth appraised values, and you get liquidity, diversification and honesty about risk in exchange.

children.text: The Rules That Shape Their Profile

markDefs.definition: Net distributable cash flows: the cash a REIT or InvIT generates from its assets after operating costs, interest and other obligations, which forms the base for distributions to unitholders.

children.text: SEBI's REIT and InvIT regulations push these vehicles towards stable, income-producing assets. Three rules matter most for their risk and return. REITs must distribute at least 90% of their

, at least 80% of a REIT's asset value must be in completed, rent-generating properties, and borrowing is capped at 49% of asset value. India's listed REITs include Embassy Office Parks, Mindspace Business Parks and Brookfield India REIT, which own mainly office parks, and Nexus Select Trust, which owns shopping malls.

children.text: Where a REIT's Return Comes From

body.latex: \text{REIT total return} \approx \text{Distribution yield} + \text{Growth in distributions} \pm \text{Change in valuation}
body.caption: The first two come from the buildings. The third comes from the market's mood and interest rates.
The building blocks of an Indian office REIT's return (illustrative)

cells: Rent from leased offices, paid out quarterly
About 6 to 7% a year at recent prices
Contracted rent escalations, re-leasing at market rents, filling vacant space and new buildings
Perhaps 3 to 5% a year, varying widely
Interest rates, office demand and investor sentiment
Can add or subtract 10 to 20% in a single year

children.text: Many Indian office leases build in a rent escalation of about 15% every three years, which works out to roughly 4.8% a year on space that stays leased. Vacancies, lease expiries and costs pull the overall growth figure down. If a REIT yields 6.5% and distributions grow 3% a year, its long-run expected return is roughly 9.5% a year, as long as the market keeps valuing it the same way. That last condition is where the listed behaviour comes in.
Listed Behaviour: The Interest Rate Lever

Investors buy REITs largely for income, so they compare the distribution yield with bond yields. When G-Sec yields rise, investors demand a higher yield from REITs too. With distributions unchanged, the only way the yield can rise is for the unit price to fall.

body.caption: Assumes the distribution per unit stays the same

body.title: When the market demands more yield
body.prompt: A REIT unit trades at a 6.5% distribution yield. Bond yields rise, and investors now demand a 7.5% yield from the REIT. If distributions stay the same, by what percentage does the unit price fall? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 6.5 ÷ 7.5 − 1 = −0.133, or about −13.3%. Not a single tenant left and not a single rupee of rent was lost, yet unitholders lost more than two years of distributions in price. This is the listed-market behaviour an appraised property fund would not show you.

body.text: The same repricing happens to directly owned property and unlisted real estate funds. Buyers there also pay less when rates rise. You just do not see it, because nobody is quoting a price every day. A REIT's volatility is not extra risk. It is the real risk made visible.

children.text: InvITs: When a High Yield Is Partly Your Own Money

markDefs.definition: The right, granted by a government authority for a fixed period, to operate an asset such as a toll road and collect its revenue. When it ends, the asset goes back to the authority.

children.text: Infrastructure Investment Trusts own roads, power transmission lines, gas pipelines and similar assets. Listed examples include IndiGrid, PowerGrid Infrastructure Investment Trust and IRB InvIT. Their yields are often higher than REIT yields, sometimes 8 to 10% or more. But many of their assets have a finite life. A toll road is usually operated under a
that ends after a fixed number of years, after which the road goes back to the government and the InvIT receives nothing more from it.

That changes what the yield means. If an asset pays ₹12 a year on ₹100 invested for 12 years and is then worth nothing, it looks like a 12% yield. But part of every payment is your own capital coming back. The true annual return is only about 6.1%.

body.caption: Same 10% yield, different remaining asset life: the true annual return on ₹100 invested (illustrative, flat distributions, zero value at the end)

body.text: Distribution yield is not total return. For a REIT that owns land and buildings indefinitely, yield plus growth is a fair estimate. For an InvIT with finite concessions, a large part of the distribution may be a return of capital. Check the remaining concession life and the break-up of each distribution into interest, dividend and capital repayment before comparing its yield with an FD.

body.caption: Key risks for REITs and InvITs

cells: Higher bond yields push unit prices down
Vacancies or weak demand for offices cut rent, as work-from-home fears did in 2020 and 2021
A few large tenants leaving can hurt distributions
Cash flows end when concessions finish; toll revenue depends on traffic
Related-party deals or buying assets from the sponsor at high prices
Debt magnifies falls in value and competes with distributions
Changes to how distributions are taxed can reduce what you keep
Wider bid-ask spreads and slippage on large orders

children.text: Tax needs particular attention. A distribution can include interest, dividends and repayment of debt or capital, each taxed differently, and the rules for some components were tightened from April 2023. Listed units held for more than 12 months qualify for long-term capital gains tax at 12.5%. Always read the tax break-up the REIT or InvIT publishes with each distribution.

body.title: Reading an InvIT yield
body.question: A road InvIT trades at an 11% distribution yield. Its main toll road concessions have about 10 years left, with no plans to acquire new assets. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: Its expected return is about 11% a year, well above an FD
Part of each distribution is likely a return of capital, so the true return could be far below 11%
The yield is guaranteed by the government, so it is risk-free
Its unit price will rise steadily as concessions near their end
body.explanation: With cash flows ending in about 10 years and no new assets, much of each payment is your own money coming back. As the table showed, even a 10% yield with 15 years left is only about 5.6% a year in true return. Unit prices tend to fall, not rise, as concessions run out.

body.title: The distribution rule
body.textWithBlank: SEBI requires a REIT to distribute at least ___% of its net distributable cash flows to unitholders.
body.explanation: The 90% rule is why REITs behave like income assets. It also means they retain little cash, so growth often requires raising new money or borrowing.

body.title: Colonel Sharma's income plan
body.scenario: Colonel Sharma (retd.), 66, lives in Dehradun and wants regular income from ₹60 lakh. He is comparing three options: bank FDs at about 7%, an office REIT at about a 6.5% distribution yield, and a road InvIT at about a 10% distribution yield. His grandson says: "Put it all in the InvIT. It pays the most every quarter."
body.prompt: How should Colonel Sharma compare the three, and what would a sensible approach look like?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Compare returns, not yields:
- FD: about 7%, with principal intact at maturity and DICGC cover up to ₹5 lakh per bank.
- REIT: about 6.5% yield plus distribution growth, so perhaps 9 to 10% a year over the long run, but with price swings along the way.
- InvIT: 10% yield, but if concessions are finite, part is return of capital. The true return depends on the remaining concession life and could be much lower.

2. Compare risks:
- REIT and InvIT unit prices can fall 10 to 20% when interest rates rise or markets sell off, which matters if he needs to sell.
- The InvIT adds traffic and concession-end risk. Its capital may shrink over time even while payouts look high.
- Distributions can be cut; FD interest cannot.

3. Compare tax: FD interest is fully taxed at his slab rate. REIT and InvIT distributions have mixed tax treatment, so the after-tax picture needs the actual break-up.

4. A sensible approach: keep the core of his income in FDs and government-backed options such as the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme. A modest slice in one or two REITs can add growing income and property diversification. If he wants an InvIT, it should be small, chosen after checking concession life and the capital-return share of distributions. Putting all ₹60 lakh in one InvIT concentrates his retirement in a single vehicle with a misleading headline yield.

cards.definition: Annual distributions per unit divided by the unit price. Not the same as total return.
Net distributable cash flows, of which a REIT must pay out at least 90%.
A contracted rent increase, commonly about 15% every three years in Indian office leases.
A time-limited right to operate an infrastructure asset. When it ends, the asset's cash flows to the InvIT stop.
Part of a distribution that gives back your own invested money rather than earning a return on it.
The entity that sets up a REIT or InvIT and transfers the initial assets to it, and often continues to hold units.

points: REITs and InvITs combine real asset cash flows, bond-like distributions and stock-like prices in one listed wrapper.
A REIT's long-run return is roughly distribution yield plus distribution growth, such as 6.5% plus 3%, but valuation changes can swing any single year by 10 to 20%.
Rising bond yields push unit prices down: a move in demanded yield from 6.5% to 7.5% cuts the price by about 13.3%.
That volatility is not extra risk; it is the same repricing that direct property hides behind appraisals.
InvITs with finite concessions can show high yields that include your own capital coming back, so 10% for 15 years is only about 5.6% a year in true return.
Watch interest rates, occupancy, concession life, sponsor governance, leverage and the tax break-up of every distribution.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell units of any REIT or InvIT named here. Yields, growth rates and returns are illustrative. SEBI regulations and tax rules can change. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before making investment decisions.
